author: Khushi Arora, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Williams Lake First Nation memorializes history and justice with opening of Sḱulé7ten Park
content:
Williams Lake First Nation Willie Sellars speaks about the significance of Sḱulé7ten park during its official opening.

Photo by Khushi Arora




This story was originally printed in the 

Williams Lake Tribune

 and appears here with minor style edits.







The Williams Lake First Nation (WLFN) celebrated the grand opening of a new memorial park in downtown Williams Lake, unveiling its name as Sḱulé7ten Park.




WLFN, also known as T’exelc, welcomed the community to the park on Oct. 13. The space memorializes WLFN’s journey towards reaching a historic specific claim settlement with “Canada.” The colonial government illegally displaced the First Nation from their traditional village site 165 years ago, in what’s now the City of Williams Lake. 




After guiding attendees through the pronunciation of the park’s name “skoo LET nn,” WLFN member William Lulua explained that the surrounding area included spaces where people did vision quests. Although there was a disconnection from the practice as Williams Lake developed into a city, he said the names of the people received through those places could not be taken away.




William Lulua shares the history and meaning behind Sḱulé7ten park’s name during the official opening on Tuesday, Oct.13. Photo by Khushi Arora

author: Jolene Banning
title: My ancestors showed me how to grieve
content:
Jolene Banning’s daughter Amber-baa, depicted through the eye of an eagle. Illustration by Jessie Boulard




Content warning: This story deals with child loss and grief. Please look after your spirit and read with care







Three years ago I was hit with a pain so deep that it seared through every fiber of my body. 




Two police officers pulled up in my driveway, driving a dark SUV, wearing dark suits and ties. They came to inform me that my child, my baby, my daughter Amber had died. 




The blow of information left me numb, stunned, separated from myself like I was watching this happen instead of partaking. 




Instantly, I became a member of a club I never wanted to belong to: of parents who have lost their children. Because I know I’m not alone in this rapidly growing group of people. It doesn’t feel natural to bury our children, so young, so beautiful. 




Amber-baa had long, shiny dark brown hair, round brown eyes, thick eyebrows and a million dollar smile — which she should, considering how much I paid the orthodontist. She was warm, caring, and fun to be around. She lit up a room and made sure everyone felt seen. And in the blink of an eye, without warning, I had lost all of that. The silence was deafening. The pain was inescapable.

author: Dionne Phillips, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Family moves into Nuxalk village site Nusq’lst for the first time in 164 years
content:
The cabin in the ancestral village of Nusq’lst. 

Submitted photo




Nestled in the lush coastal temperate rainforest of the Bella Coola Valley sits the ancestral village of Nusq’lst.




The last time someone lived at the historic Nuxalk townsite was in 

1862

, as people’s forced removal from their homelands and the devastating smallpox epidemic emptied many traditional villages.




Now, 164 years later, three generations of a family are calling Nusq’lst home again. 




Kmalsuuncw (Orden Mack) and his mother Nuskmata turned what was originally planned as a hand-built hunting cabin into a permanent family home when Kmalsuuncw became a new father.




Building the cabin quickly became a family project, with Kmalsuuncw receiving advice on its construction from cousins, uncles and other supporters.




“We’ve received a lot of community support, and honestly, that’s been a really driving feature as to why we kept on going for as long as we did,” he said in an interview with IndigiNews. 




Kmalsuuncw notes the site holds much of his family’s origin story. The village site’s name Nusq’lst was his grandfather — Nuskmata’s late father’s — name.

author: Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: As parts of the Nicola River run dry, a father fears what his children will inherit
content:
Brian Holmes, a councillor for the Upper Nicola Band, walks through a dry stretch of the Nicola River on Sept. 18, 2026, a few minutes downstream from his community of spaxmn (Douglas Lake) in the Nicola Valley, in B.C.’s southern interior. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




On this stretch of the Nicola River, Brian Holmes misses the sound of water. 




“This is heartbreaking,” he quietly says to himself as he prepares to park above a kilometre-long stretch where no surface water remains.




In the absence of the river’s flow, birds can be heard in the thick vegetation, their calls occasionally joined by a horse neighing in the distance or a car passing along Douglas Lake Road above.




The 44-year-old Upper Nicola Band (UNB) member and father of two leaves his vehicle and disappears into the bush separating the river from a small ranch below the road, a few minutes downstream from his community of spaxmn (Douglas Lake) in the Nicola Valley, in “B.C.’s” southern interior. 




He re-emerges from the bush and makes his way down a steep slope into the exposed riverbed, where large boulders rise from a channel that should be running with water on this warm mid-September morning.

author: Jeremy Appel, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Indigenous rights at forefront of anti-AI data centre rally in ‘Edmonton’
content:
Chief Sheldon Sunshine of Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation speaks at an Oct. 3 rally against data centres outside the ‘Alberta’ legislature building in amiskwacîwâskahikan (Edmonton). 

Photo by Jeremy Appel




This story was originally published in 

Alberta Native News

 on Oct. 6, 

and appears here with permission and style edits

, 

with added context from the author’s 

earlier article

 from May 14

.







More than 100 people gathered outside the Legislative Assembly building in amiskwacîwâskahikan (Edmonton) on Oct. 3 to protest the provincial and federal governments’ permissive approach towards building artificial intelligence data centres.  




Elder Taz Bouchier opened the rally with a land acknowledgement before tying the proposed 7.5-gigawatt Wonder Valley data centre near Grande Prairie’s potential water usage to the oil industry’s plans to release treated tailings fluids into the Athabasca watershed. 




“When did people lose sight of how valuable water is to living? When money came into play. That’s all these data centers are about,” said Bouchier. 




Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation is challenging the province’s decision to award a water license of 24-million cubic metres to the Municipal District of Greenview for Wonder Valley without consulting the Treaty 8 First Nation, which relies on the Smoky River for its water.

author: Brittany Boschman, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: A century after it was taken, ancestral tipi cover returns to Kawacatoose First Nation
content:
Using wooden pins and great care, Kawacatoose First Nation members fasten an Ancestor’s painted tipi cover on Aug. 28, after it was finally returned to their Saskatchewan community from ‘Washington, D.C.’ 

Photo by Brittany Boschman




“We’re gonna take you home now.”




Those were okimâw (Chief) Cory Dustyhorn’s words when he first touched the tipi cover connected to his great-great-great-grandfather, sîpiskwêsîkan.




After a century away from 

Kawacatoose First Nation

, the ancestral item has returned to the Cree community.




Community and family members gathered around the tipi cover after it was brought back from the 

Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of the American Indian

 in “Washington, D.C.” 




They prayed over it and welcomed it home.




“When I first touched it, I just felt so emotional,” Dustyhorn said. 




“I was thinking of all those that are gone on before me.”




He thought about his parents, grandparents and ancestors — who preserved the history of the item through generations.




He prayed for them to be present as the community finally brought home a piece of their history. 




“I told all of them, ‘Come with us, come and attend with us,” Dustyhorn recalled. 




“I know they were in between all of us — and they were here, too.”




Members of the Dustyhorn family and supporters celebrate the return of their Ancestor sîpiskwêsîkan’s

author: Taina Da Silva
title: Near Grassy Narrows, an Elder shows us how using the land also protects it
content:
Anishinaabe Elder Gwawich’s Land Back Garden on the outskirts of the Grassy Narrows First Nation. Photo by Taina Da Silva




I’m thinking about the power of my treaty rights as I drive to meet with Anishinaabe Elder Gwawich — Roberta Keesick — on a late summer day on the outskirts of Grassy Narrows.




Gwawich is an activist and trapper who has substantial experience of being on the land and creating land-based learning systems for our community. She grew up in our territory with a traditional Anishinaabek family, and she works to restore our traditional ways. 




As I pull into the site, Gwawich offers me some ripe vegetables — a squash, green beans and tomatoes — that she’s harvested from an extensive garden nearby. 




Gwawich and I are ten minutes outside of the reserve line of Grassy Narrows First Nation, a small and semi-remote community in northwestern Ontario. We sit at an off-grid campsite and community garden which Gwawich started by herself to host her Seven Grandfathers Teachings Program.




The Seven Grandfather Teachings — love, respect, bravery, truth, honesty, humility, and wisdom — are what Gwawich’s social program follows, and she hopes her program will impact Grassy in a way that will bring us Anishinaabek back to the land and culture. 




“Colonization has changed our ways of thinking,” she says.

author: Daniel Opasinis, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Grassy Narrows River Run brings demands for mercury justice to Tkarón:to
content:
On Wednesday, Sept. 23, members of Grassy Narrows First Nation, Whitedog, and organizers in Tkarón:to came together for the annual Grassy Narrows River Run. Photo by Daniel Opasinis




On the front lawn of Queen’s Park in Tkarón:to stands a tall statue of Sir James Pliny Whitney, Ontario premier from 1905 to 1914, whose government promoted mining and forestry development in northern Ontario.




Over a century later, Glenn Cameron, councillor for Wabaseemoong First Nation (Whitedog), stood below that same statue. Holding a microphone connected to a portable sound system, he addressed a crowd gathered to demand action on the mercury contamination that continues to affect his community.




On Wednesday, Sept. 23, members of Grassy Narrows First Nation, Whitedog, and organizers in Tkarón:to came together for the annual Grassy Narrows River Run. They are calling on Ontario and “Canada” to fairly compensate people in Grassy Narrows 

for the mercury crisis and stop the Dryden mill

.




People rally for justice for Grassy Narrows in Toronto on Sept. 23. Photo by Daniel Opasinis




Between 

1962 and 1970

, Dryden Chemicals Limited discharged approximately nine tonnes of mercury into the Wabigoon River. The contamination spread through the river system, poisoning fish that people in Grassy Narrows and Wabaseemoong relied on for food and their livelihoods.

author: IndigiNews Staff
title: In photos: Nations mark Orange Shirt Day in Manitoba, Saskatchewan
content:
Daniella Peltier with an Every Child Matters flag at the Southern Chiefs’ Organization’s Orange Shirt Day powwow at the Canada Life Centre in Winnipeg on September 30. Photo by Crystal Greene




Indigenous communities across “Canada” marked the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation — also known as Orange Shirt Day — with various gatherings and events on Sept. 30.




On the prairies, IndigiNews reporters Crystal Greene and Brittany Boschman attended gatherings in or near their own communities. Both reporters photographed the day’s events, capturing the spirit of each and honouring their own connections to the story.




In Winnipeg, Crystal attended a commemorative walk and powwow that was hosted by the Southern Chiefs’ Organization at Canada Life Centre.




In Saskatchewan in the Qu’Appelle Valley, Brittany was present for a community gathering and walk hosted by the Star Blanket Cree Nation. You can find a selection of their photos below.







Women who survived residential “schools” took part in a powwow dance special, honouring survivors in Winnipeg on Orange Shirt Day. Photos by Crystal Greene




Male survivors of residential “schools” were also honoured during a dance special at the Winnipeg Orange Shirt Day powwow. Photo by Crystal Greene




There was a sea of orange, interspersed with powwow dancers, during the intertribal dances of the Orange Shirt Day powwow

author: Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: In Tk̓emlúps, community gathers to ‘reclaim our space’ and denounce white nationalism
content:
At the same site where a white nationalist demonstration occurred in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc on Sunday, more than 100 Secwépemc people and their allies returned to the area two days later to reclaim the space. They drummed, sang and prayed to cleanse the spot, which is located a few hundred metres away from the former Kamloops Indian Residential School. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Content warning: This article contains details about residential “schools.” Please read with care for your spirit.







On the eve of Orange Shirt Day, more than 100 people gathered in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc to cleanse and reclaim a site where a white nationalist demonstration occurred earlier this week.




For nearly three hours on Tuesday night, Secwépemc people and their allies drummed, sang and prayed — for the land and the people, and for all the families impacted by residential “schools.”




Secwépemc people and their allies drum, sing and pray on Tuesday, near the site where a white nationalist demonstration took place in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc two days prior. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Ashley Michel from Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc organized Tuesday’s gathering with four other Secwépemc (Shuswap) mothers.

author: Crystal Greene, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: New book aims to ‘push back and defend survivors’ against denialism
content:
Pre-signed copies of ‘Truth Before Reconciliation’ were made available for audience goers of the September 17 launch in Winnipeg. Photo by Crystal Greene




Outside a Winnipeg bookstore, about 25 volunteers in orange shirts formed a welcoming line as sage smoke rose from an abalone shell. 




Inside McNally Robinson Booksellers, more than 300 people gathered for the launch of 

Truth Before Reconciliation: Confronting Residential School Denialism

. Outside, the volunteers helped provide security as organizers anticipated denialists might try to disrupt the event on September 17. 




“We want to make sure that it’s safe for the survivors,” said Emma Tardiff, one of the volunteers. “I really care about my community.”




Published by University of Manitoba Press ahead of National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, the collection grew from an effort by scholars and authors to confront the denial and downplaying of what survivors experienced. 




The book consists of 13 chapters that include survivor interviews, expert analysis and examination of the denialism movement. Contributors include historians, educators, survivors, archivists and archaeologists, alongside the book’s two co-editors, Sean Carlton and Niigaan Sinclair.

author: Dionne Phillips, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Indigenous New York Fashion Week brings family and futurity to the runway
content:
Details at Cheyenne LeGrande’s show at Indigenous NYFW on Sept. 11. Photo by Dionne Philips




Backstage at Indigenous New York Fashion Week (INYFW), Dusty LeGrande helped lace up garments from his sibling Cheyenne Rain LeGrande’s collection. A year earlier, Cheyenne had been there to model and help him with his own designs.




“It’s kind of so special because now he’s backstage with me, helping me lace up these garments, and it’s kind of nice that we can help each other out in that way,” she told IndigiNews.




The artist from Bigstone Cree Nation closed the Emerging Voices show on Sept. 11 with a collection that included laced-up mini skirts, tops with jingle dress cones and a wearable art piece made from 3,300 pop can tabs and ribbons.




A model showcasing LeGrande’s designs including the piece made from pop tabs and ribbons. Photo by Dionne Phillips




INYFW’s second year ran from Sept. 10 to 15, bringing together 30 Indigenous designers for six shows in Lenapehoking (Lenape homelands), on the island Mannahatta (Manhattan).




Just off Fashion Avenue, the American Indian Community House was transformed for the event, with seats lining the runway and fabric cascading to the floor.




Korina Emmerich (Puyallup descent) and Liana Shewey (Mvskoke), co-founders of Relative Arts and INYFW, organized the event with volunteers and professionals.

author: Frey Blake-Pijogge, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: In a changing northern landscape, Inuit bear guards keep people safe in the wilderness
content:
A nanuk (polar bear) in Tongait KakKasuangita SilakKijapvinga (Torngat Mountains National Park) in northern ‘Labrador.’ 

Photo by Frey Blake-Pijogge




After retiring from his career as a federal conservation officer, Derrick Pottle — an Inuk Elder from Tikigâksuagusik (Rigolet) — devoted himself to guiding people on the land, carving, hunting, and training bear guards.




The seasoned instructor and guide founded BearSafe Planning in 2005, which trains and certifies students to perform the role of guarding for the bear species found in the region and beyond — including polar bears, grizzly bears and black bears. 




Pottle’s three-day course is advertised as offering “safety, protection, confidence in bear country.” Bear guards work to monitor for bears  and prevent encounters with humans out on the land.




“The whole objective of the course,” he told IndigiNews, is firstly “people’s safety” around bears. But that aim “is followed very closely” by “bear safety,” he explained.




“We want to prepare people … to recognize some of the potential signs that the bear is not comfortable,” he continued. “They may feel threatened, they may feel intimidated, and they may even charge or attack you.”




He teaches his students “how to recognize those signs, how to prepare yourself for them, the tools you have to use to do your job.”

author: Santana Dreaver
title: After more than a century, this Salish woolly dog pelt has returned to ‘B.C.’
content:
Only known pelt of the extinct woolly dog. Photo by Brittany M. Hance, courtesy of Division of Mammals, Smithsonian

Institution 




This story is co-published 

with the Narwhal

 as part of their 

2026 Indigenous journalism fellowship







Coming face to face with the pelt of a now-extinct Salish woolly dog was an emotional experience for Jordan Wilson.




The curator from xʷməθkʷəy̓əm (Musqueam Indian Band) attended an unveiling at the Museum of Anthropology in “Vancouver” as the ancestor was welcomed back to its home territories earlier this month.




The pelt is on loan from the Smithsonian institution, where it was in storage for more than a century — it was sent to the “American” museum in 1859. It will be at MOA until August of 2027. 




Belonging to a dog from Stó:lō territories known as Mutton, it’s the only known Salish woolly dog pelt in existence.




As the pelt was unveiled to its Salish relatives on Sept. 4, Wilson attended along with other Salish community members from “Vancouver Island” and the “Fraser Valley.”




“For me personally, I was caught off guard at the emotional quality of it,” Wilson said.




“Seeing this pelt in person, seeing its little paws and seeing its little nose, realizing that this was a living being that was alive 160 years ago.”
